pos: n. (safe keeping; protection; a guard that secures)
etymology: Hebrew mishmereth, a watch, a charge, a thing kept — from shamar, to keep or guard. The English compounds safe with guard: a keeping that secures.
biblical_def: Abide thou with me, fear not: for he that seeketh my life seeketh thy life: but with me thou shalt be in safeguard. David says this to Abiathar, the one priest who escaped Saul's slaughter at Nob, and the circumstances make it one of the strangest offers of security in Scripture. David is a fugitive with a price on his head, living in caves, hunted by a king with an army. He has no fortress, no troops to spare, and no legal standing. He also has just accepted responsibility for the massacre: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house. What he offers is not safety from danger but shared danger under the man God has anointed — he that seeketh my life seeketh thy life — and he calls that safeguard. The logic is covenantal rather than tactical. To be with David is to be on the side God has committed himself to, and the narrative bears it out: Saul sought him every day, but God delivered him not into his hand. The pattern runs through Scripture and is the ground of every promise of refuge. Safety is not a location or a circumstance but a person: he that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. The safest place available to Abiathar was beside a hunted man who had God's word on him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): defense; protection; security; a convoy or guard to protect a traveler or property.
webster_full: SAFEGUARD, n. That which defends or protects; defense; protection.
SAFEGUARD, n. A convoy or guard to protect a traveler or goods; a passport; a warrant of security.
SAFEGUARD, v.t. To guard; to protect.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
PROTECTION, n. Defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss, injury or annoyance.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 22:23
Abide thou with me, fear not: for he that seeketh my life seeketh thy life: but with me thou shalt be in safeguard.
1 Samuel 22:22
And David said unto Abiathar, I knew it that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house.
1 Samuel 23:14
And David abode in the wilderness in strong holds, and remained in a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God delivered him not into his hand.
Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
corruption_summary: Safety is understood as the absence of danger, and God's protection is taken as a promise of that; Scripture locates safeguard in a person and repeatedly places his people in danger while keeping them.
corruption_paragraphs: The promises of divine protection are widely read as guarantees of outcome — that a believer who trusts God will not suffer the harm he fears. Psalm 91 is quoted this way constantly, generally by people who have not noticed that Satan quoted it that way first, in the wilderness, and was answered with a rebuke. David's offer to Abiathar is the corrective in narrative form. He promises no reduction in danger; he promises that the danger will be shared and that the man will be kept. Scripture's martyrs were kept in precisely this sense, and so was Daniel's generation, whose three friends said their God was able to deliver them and that they would not serve the image if he did not.

The contrary error drains the promises of any concrete content, treating protection as a purely inward serenity with no bearing on actual events. That is not the Bible either. God really did keep David out of Saul's hand, day after day, in a narrative that says so plainly. Providence is particular, and the Reformed doctrine holds that not a sparrow falls without the Father, and that the very hairs of the head are numbered. The believer's confidence rests on a God who governs real events, and his safety consists in belonging to the One who governs them — which is why the safeguard held out here is with me rather than away from here.

pos: n. (defence; shelter; a covering from harm)
etymology: Hebrew sithrah, a covering or hiding place, from sathar, to hide. Latin protectio, from protegere, to cover in front. In its one appearance the word is spoken with heavy irony, of idols invited to do what they cannot.
biblical_def: Which did eat the fat of their sacrifices, and drank the wine of their drink offerings? let them rise up and help you, and be your protection. The Song of Moses reaches its sharpest point here, and the tone is scorn. God has asked where the gods are in whom Israel trusted, and now he invites them to act: let them get up, let them help, let them be your protection. The irony is directed at the whole logic of idolatry. These gods have been fed — they ate the fat and drank the wine of the offerings — and the transaction assumed by every pagan system is that feeding the god secures the god's help. Moses invites the creditors to collect, and nothing happens. The psalmist states the reason in flat prose: their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands, and, they that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them. An idol cannot protect because it has no life of its own; it is downstream of its worshippers. Against this God sets his own declaration in the very next verse, and it is one of the great statements of the divine uniqueness and sovereignty in the Old Testament: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand. Protection in Scripture belongs only to the God who is not fed by anyone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss, injury or annoyance; that which preserves from injury.
webster_full: PROTECTION, n. Defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss, injury or annoyance.
PROTECTION, n. That which protects or preserves from injury.
PROTECT, v.t. To cover or shield from danger or injury; to defend; to guard; to preserve in safety.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:38
Which did eat the fat of their sacrifices, and drank the wine of their drink offerings? let them rise up and help you, and be your protection.
Deuteronomy 32:39
See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand.
Psalm 115:4
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Psalm 115:8
They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as a primitive error about statues; Moses exposes it as a transaction — feeding a god to secure its help — and that transaction survives wherever religion is practised as leverage on God.
corruption_paragraphs: The mockery in Deuteronomy 32:38 is aimed at the mechanism, not the material. What made these gods attractive was not that they were carved but that they could be fed, and a god who can be fed can be managed. That is the enduring appeal of idolatry and it does not require a statue. The prosperity teaching runs on exactly this logic — the offering given to secure the return, the faith deployed to obtain the outcome — and so does any piety in which devotion is performed to make God act. Moses' challenge applies to all of it: let them rise up and help you. A god one can bind is a god who cannot save.

The doctrine set against the idols is unusually stark, and it is God's own speech: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand. Modern discomfort with that sentence is considerable, and the usual remedies are to soften the verbs or to assign the wounding to other agents. Scripture does not permit either. The God who protects is the God who wounds, and the doctrine of providence is not the claim that only pleasant things come from him. What the verse gives the believer is the only real ground of safety: no other hand can reach him, because there is no power that can deliver out of the hand that holds him.

pos: n. (a place of repose; the fold where a flock lies down)
etymology: Hebrew rebets, a place of lying down, from rabats, to crouch or lie down — used of flocks settling in a fold. The Authorized Version writes it as one word; the image throughout is pastoral.
biblical_def: My people hath been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray, they have turned them away on the mountains: they have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their restingplace. The indictment falls on the shepherds first, and the sequence is precise. The sheep are lost, but they are lost because those set over them caused them to go astray. The wandering follows: from mountain to hill, a picture of restless movement with no fold at the end of it. And the final clause names the real loss — they have forgotten their restingplace. The Hebrew rebets is where a flock lies down, and lying down is the sign that a sheep feels safe; a flock that will not lie down is a flock that has no shepherd it trusts. This is the language of the twenty-third psalm from the far side: he maketh me to lie down in green pastures. Jeremiah adds the consequence in the next verse, that all who found them devoured them, and that their adversaries excused themselves by saying, We offend not, because they have sinned against the LORD, the habitation of justice. The remedy runs through the whole of Scripture in the same pastoral vocabulary, and the Lord speaks it directly: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Hebrews holds out the same thing as still future and still open: there remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under RESTING-PLACE: a place for rest; a place where repose may be had.
webster_full: RESTING-PLACE, n. A place for rest; a place where rest or repose may be obtained.
REST, n. Cessation of motion or action of any kind; quiet; repose; a state of quiet.
REST, n. Sleep; also, the final sleep; death; and hence, quiet, peace, or happiness in a future life.
FOLD, n. A pen or inclosure for sheep; a place where a flock of sheep is kept.
SHEPHERD, n. One who has the care of a flock; figuratively, a pastor, a minister of the gospel.
scriptures: Jeremiah 50:6

My people hath been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray, they have turned them away on the mountains: they have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their restingplace.
Psalm 23:2
He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Matthew 11:28
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Hebrews 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
corruption_summary: Rest is widely reduced to leisure or to the management of stress, and the responsibility of shepherds for a wandering flock is quietly dropped; Jeremiah assigns the blame first to the leaders.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account of rest treats it as recovery — time away, balance restored, stress managed — and there is a real creational goodness in sleep and sabbath that Scripture affirms without embarrassment. But the rest Jeremiah's sheep have forgotten is not a break from work. It is a place to lie down, and lying down in the pastoral image is what an animal does when it is not afraid. The Lord offers that to the labouring and heavy laden, and the offer terminates on himself: come unto me. A believer who has managed his schedule and not come to Christ has arranged his exhaustion more comfortably.

The verse is also a warning to those who teach, and it is not softened anywhere in Scripture. Their shepherds have caused them to go astray — the flock is lost, and the responsibility is assigned upward. Ezekiel devotes a chapter to the same charge, and James warns that teachers shall receive the greater condemnation. Where a congregation is restless, unfed, and moving from one thing to the next, the first question the Bible asks is not about the sheep. It is a hard word for ministers, and its hardness is exactly proportioned to the seriousness of the office.

pos: n. (the act of rising up; getting up from rest)
etymology: Hebrew qum, to rise or stand up. The Authorized Version pairs it with downsitting to render a Hebrew idiom for the whole of ordinary life — sitting down and getting up, the two commonest acts a body performs.
biblical_def: Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. The pairing is an idiom, and it is chosen for its ordinariness. Downsitting and uprising are not significant events; they are what a man does dozens of times a day without noticing. David is saying that God's knowledge of him extends to the parts of his life that are too trivial to record. The psalm then moves inward in the same breath — thou understandest my thought afar off — and outward in the verses following: thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. The doctrine is omniscience, and David develops it in the most personal terms available: God's knowledge of him is exhaustive, immediate, and comfortable rather than threatening. That last point is where the psalm differs sharply from the modern instinct. Being fully known is now widely experienced as exposure; David treats it as the ground of security, which is why the psalm that begins with total knowledge ends with an invitation to more of it — Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts. A man who has something to hide does not pray that. The middle of the psalm draws the further conclusion that there is nowhere outside this knowledge: whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under UPRISING: the act of rising; act of rising up; ascent.
webster_full: UPRISING, n. The act of rising; act of rising up.
UPRISE, v.i. To rise from a bed or seat; to get up.
DOWNSITTING, n. The act of sitting down; repose; a resting.
OMNISCIENCE, n. The knowledge of all things; infinite or unbounded knowledge; an attribute of God only.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through for the purpose of finding something; to examine; to explore.
scriptures: Psalm 139:2
Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off.
Psalm 139:1
O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.
Psalm 139:3
Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways.
Psalm 139:7
Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
corruption_summary: Divine omniscience is denied outright by open theism and felt as surveillance by a culture that prizes privacy; David treats exhaustive knowledge as the ground of comfort and asks for more of it.
corruption_paragraphs: Open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, holds that God does not exhaustively know the future free acts of his creatures, and adjusts the doctrine of omniscience accordingly. Psalm 139 makes that adjustment difficult. God knows the psalmist's thought afar off, is acquainted with all his ways, and — in the verses that follow — saw his substance yet being unperfect, and in God's book all his members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them. That is knowledge of a life before it was lived. The classical doctrine is not a philosophical imposition on the text; the text is where the doctrine comes from.

The cultural resistance is different and more widely felt. In an age formed by surveillance, to be fully known sounds like exposure, and the psalm is read with a shiver. David's response runs the other way, and it ends in a request: Search me, O God, and know my heart. The difference is not temperament but standing. A man under judgment fears to be known; a man in covenant with God finds that being known is the only ground on which he can be loved as he actually is, rather than as he has presented himself. The doctrine cuts both ways, as the psalm itself acknowledges in its severe middle section, and the believer's comfort is that the One who misses nothing has set his love on him anyway.

“whither shall I flee from thy presence?” — nowhere outside it.

pos: v. (to thrust or immerse suddenly, as into water or mire)
etymology: Hebrew tabal, to dip or immerse — the same verb used of dipping in blood or water in the ceremonial law. Old French plongier, from Latin plumbum, lead: to sink as a plummet sinks.
biblical_def: Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me. Job is answering the argument that a man may simply clear himself before God, and he does it by pressing the logic to its end. He has just said, if I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean, then comes this verse: even so, God could plunge him in the ditch until his own clothes recoiled from him. The image is deliberately grotesque and the point is exact. Self-cleansing is worthless before a holy God, because the standard is not the man's estimate of himself but God's. Job is not accusing God of injustice here so much as measuring the distance. And he names the real difficulty in the verses that follow, in words that reach further than he knew: for he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment. Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both. A daysman is an umpire or mediator, and Job's complaint is that no such person exists — there is no one qualified to stand between God and man, touching both. The whole of the New Testament answers that complaint: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. Job asked for someone who could lay a hand on both parties, and the incarnation is the answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to thrust into water or other fluid; to immerse; to cast into water or mire; to overwhelm.
webster_full: PLUNGE, v.t. To thrust into water or other fluid substance, or into any substance that is penetrable; to immerse in a fluid.
PLUNGE, v.t. To thrust or drive into any state in which the thing is considered as enveloped or surrounded; as, to plunge one in distress.
PLUNGE, n. The act of thrusting into water or any penetrable substance; difficulty; strait.
DITCH, n. A trench in the earth made by digging; a moat; a channel for water.
DAYSMAN, n. An umpire or arbiter; a mediator.
scriptures: Job 9:31
Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me.
Job 9:30
If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean;
Job 9:32
For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment.
Job 9:33
Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both.
corruption_summary: Self-cleansing remains the default religion of the natural heart, and Job's complaint that no mediator exists is answered only by the incarnation, which modern theologies weaken wherever Christ's true deity or true humanity is softened.
corruption_paragraphs: Every religion of works is an attempt at the washing Job describes, and his verdict on it is the Bible's. Snow water and clean hands leave a man where he started, because the problem is not the state of his hands but the holiness of the One he must answer to. Isaiah says the same in the image of filthy rags, and Paul in the flat declaration that by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight. This is not a low view of human effort; it is a high view of God. Job is being more realistic than his comforters, not more despairing.

The daysman Job says does not exist is the centre of the Christian faith, and the doctrine that supplies him is precise: one Person, two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation. Every softening of that costs the mediator. An Arian Christ cannot lay a hand on God; a merely apparent humanity cannot lay a hand on man; a Christ who is a great teacher or moral example is not an umpire between parties but a third party with no standing. Job's requirement was that one person touch both, and Chalcedon states what must be true of anyone who does. The complaint of Job 9 is the reason the church has always fought over Christology rather than treating it as a technicality.

“neither is there any daysman betwixt us” — the lack the incarnation answers.

pos: v. (to stir up; to wake a resting beast)
etymology: Hebrew qum, to rise, in a causative form — to make to rise. The English rouse is a hunting term: to drive a beast from its lair. The word appears in Jacob's blessing on Judah, and the beast in question is a lion.
biblical_def: Judah is a lion's whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up? Jacob is blessing his sons at the end of his life, and the blessing on Judah is the one the whole Bible follows. The picture is of a lion that has fed and lain down, and the question <em>who shall rouse him up?</em ; is rhetorical — nobody willingly disturbs a lion at rest. Strength at rest is more formidable than strength in motion, because it has nothing to prove. Balaam repeats the figure almost word for word over Israel: he couched, he lay down as a lion, and as a great lion: who shall stir him up? Then Jacob's blessing continues into explicit prophecy: the sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be. That is a promise of kingship in Judah's line running forward to one who comes, and the New Testament takes it up without hesitation. When John weeps in heaven because no man is found worthy to open the book, the elder's comfort is a title: Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book. And what John turns to see is a Lamb as it had been slain. The lion of Judah and the slain Lamb are the same Person, which is the whole gospel in one image.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to excite to thought or action from a state of rest; to wake from sleep or repose; to drive a beast from his lair.
webster_full: ROUSE, v.t. To wake from sleep or repose; to excite to thought or action from a state of rest.
ROUSE, v.t. To put in action; to agitate; to drive from a lurking place.
ROUSE, v.t. In hunting, to start from a thicket or covert; as, to rouse a deer or a lion.
WHELP, n. The young of the canine species, and of several other beasts of prey; a puppy; a young lion.
COUCH, v.i. To lie down, as on a bed or place of repose; to lie down, as a beast.
scriptures: Genesis 49:9
Judah is a lion's whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up?
Numbers 24:9
He couched, he lay down as a lion, and as a great lion: who shall stir him up? Blessed is he that blesseth thee, and cursed is he that curseth thee.
Revelation 5:5
And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.
Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
corruption_summary: Messianic prophecy in the patriarchal blessings is commonly reassigned to later editors writing after the fact, and the lion imagery is detached from the Lamb it belongs with.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical treatment of Genesis 49 dates the blessing late and reads it as a retrojection composed after the rise of the Davidic monarchy — prophecy written backwards to explain a political outcome. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship of the Torah and takes the blessing as what it presents itself to be: Jacob's words to his sons, given under inspiration, looking forward. The alternative requires that the whole canonical presentation be a literary device, and it cannot explain why a late writer inventing a pedigree would include the surrounding material about Reuben's incest, Simeon and Levi's treachery, and Judah's own disgrace in Genesis 38.

The devotional misuse is nearly the opposite and is common in churches that prize strength: the Lion of Judah taken as a warrant for a triumphalist Christianity, all conquest and no cross. Revelation 5 forecloses it in the space of two verses. John is told to behold the Lion, and what he sees when he turns is a Lamb as it had been slain. The two images are not alternatives held in balance; they are one Person, and the Lion prevails because he was slain. Jacob's lion at rest is not a picture of force but of a settled strength that need not be demonstrated, and the church waits on a King who has already conquered by dying.

Hebrew rabats (H7257) — to crouch, to lie down; rendered couched.
Hebrew Shiloh (H7886) — he whose it is; the one until whose coming the sceptre remains.
Greek leon (G3023) — a lion; the Lion of the tribe of Juda at Revelation 5:5.

“he couched, he lay down as a lion” — Balaam repeating the figure over Israel.
“the Lion of the tribe of Juda… hath prevailed” — and John sees a Lamb.

pos: n. (steadfastness; firmness; the quality of standing)
etymology: Hebrew emunah, firmness, faithfulness, steadiness — from aman, to be firm or trustworthy, the root of amen. Latin stabilitas, from stare, to stand.
biblical_def: And wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation: the fear of the LORD is his treasure. Isaiah is speaking to a nation under Assyrian threat, and the promise addresses exactly what such a nation wants: the stability of thy times. What is striking is what he names as the source of it. Not walls, not treaties, not an army — but wisdom and knowledge, and behind them the fear of the LORD, which he calls his treasure. The Hebrew emunah means firmness and faithfulness together; a stable time is one that can be relied on because it rests on something that does not shift. Isaiah has just said in the preceding verse that the LORD is exalted; for he dwelleth on high: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. The order is the order the whole Bible keeps: God is high, and therefore the times can be steady. And the last clause supplies the hinge, since the fear of the LORD is where wisdom begins — the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding. Stability in Scripture is therefore never a property a society achieves by arrangement. It is downstream of what a people fears. A nation that fears God has a foundation under its times; a nation that fears something else has borrowed its stability from whatever it fears, and will lose it on the same terms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): steadiness; stableness; firmness; strength to stand without being moved or overthrown; steadiness of purpose.
webster_full: STABILITY, n. Steadiness; stableness; firmness; strength to stand without being moved or overthrown.
STABILITY, n. Steadiness of purpose; firmness of resolution; constancy.
STABLE, a. Fixed; firmly established; not to be easily moved, shaken or overthrown.
WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; the choice of laudable ends, and of the best means to accomplish them.
TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve; something very much valued.
scriptures: Isaiah 33:6
And wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation: the fear of the LORD is his treasure.
Isaiah 33:5
The LORD is exalted; for he dwelleth on high: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness.
Proverbs 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Psalm 111:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.
corruption_summary: Social stability is sought through policy, prosperity, and security arrangements; Isaiah grounds it in wisdom and knowledge that begin in the fear of the LORD, and treats that fear as the nation's actual treasure.
corruption_paragraphs: Every political order proposes its own foundation for stable times — economic growth, the right institutions, security, education understood as technique. Isaiah does not deny that governments govern, and Scripture honours the civil magistrate as one of the three God-ordained authorities alongside family and church. What he denies is that stability can be manufactured at that level. Wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and the wisdom in view is the wisdom that begins in the fear of the LORD. A people may have every instrument of order and lack the one thing that makes order hold.

The claim cuts against a common churchly instinct as well, which is to treat the fear of God as a private matter with no public consequence — the Radical Two-Kingdoms move, in which the civil sphere is governed by reason alone and Christ's lordship is confined to the church. Isaiah addresses a nation, and the treasure he names is a national one. The dictionary affirms the classical two-kingdoms doctrine of the Reformers, in which the spheres are genuinely distinct and Christ is nonetheless Lord of both, and it declines the modern narrowing. The alternative to the fear of God in public life is not neutrality; it is the fear of something else.
roots_summary: Hebrew emunah (H530), firmness, faithfulness; aman (H539), to be firm or reliable; chokmah (H2451), wisdom; yirah (H3374), fear or reverence.
roots_lines: Hebrew emunah (H530) — firmness, steadiness, faithfulness; rendered stability.
Hebrew aman (H539) — to be firm, to trust; the root that gives amen.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, skill in living; the first of the two named supports.
Hebrew daath (H1847) — knowledge; the second.
Hebrew yirah (H3374) — fear, reverence; called the nation's treasure.
usage: “the stability of thy times” — what a threatened nation wants.
“wisdom and knowledge” — named as its source.
“the fear of the LORD is his treasure” — the hinge of the promise.

pos: n. pl. (markers set along a road; guideposts)
etymology: Hebrew tsiyun, a signpost or monument, from tsiyah, to mark — a pillar set up so that a road can be found again. The Authorized Version's compound is exact: marks of the way.
biblical_def: Set thee up waymarks, make thee high heaps: set thine heart toward the highway, even the way which thou wentest: turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities. God is speaking to a people going into exile, and the command is startlingly practical. As you go, mark the road. Set up pillars and pile up heaps of stones, so that the way out can be found again as the way back. Behind the instruction is a promise: the exiles will return, and the road they are walking in sorrow is the road they will walk home. Two things in the verse are worth dwelling on. The marking is their work — set thee up, make thee — while the return is God's doing and God's call, turn again, repeated twice. And the instruction is addressed to the heart as well as the hands: set thine heart toward the highway. A people can walk a road without ever intending to come back; God tells them to keep the direction in mind. The same prophet elsewhere describes the identical posture for a people who have lost their way: stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. Waymarks are for finding a road that already exists. Scripture's consistent counsel to the wandering is not to strike out but to go back to the way that was there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under WAY-MARK: a mark to guide in traveling; a monument or sign set up to direct the way.
webster_full: WAY-MARK, n. A mark to guide in traveling; a monument or sign set up to point out the road.
WAY, n. A passing; a road, street, or path; course; direction of motion or travel.
HIGHWAY, n. A public road; a way open to all passengers.
MONUMENT, n. Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated.
HEAP, n. A pile or mass; a collection of things laid in a body so as to form an elevation.
scriptures: Jeremiah 31:21
Set thee up waymarks, make thee high heaps: set thine heart toward the highway, even the way which thou wentest: turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities.
Jeremiah 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Jeremiah 31:22
How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter? for the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man.
Jeremiah 31:33

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
corruption_summary: Novelty is prized in doctrine and practice, and the old paths are treated as nostalgia; Jeremiah sets waymarks precisely so that a road already walked can be found again.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct of each generation is to believe that its situation is unprecedented and that the received way therefore needs replacing. Jeremiah's counsel is the reverse: ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein. The waymarks exist because the road exists — it does not need to be invented, only found. This is the reason confessions matter. The 1689 and the Westminster are not repositories of sentiment but heaps of stones piled by people who had walked the road, and a church that will not consult them is choosing to navigate an ancient country without a map because the map is old.

The opposite failure is to treat the waymarks as the destination. Stones piled beside a road are worthless to a man who admires them and does not walk. Jeremiah 6:16 ends with the sentence that makes the whole passage a warning rather than a comfort — but they said, We will not walk therein. A congregation can be entirely correct about the old paths and standing still on them. And the chapter itself refuses mere restoration as the final hope: a few verses after the waymarks comes the new covenant, in which God writes the law in the heart, which is the only thing that finally makes a people walk.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsiyun (H6725), a signpost or waymark; tamrur (H8564), a pillar or high heap; mesillah (H4546), a highway; shub (H7725), to turn again.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsiyun (H6725) — a marker, a signpost; rendered waymarks.
Hebrew tamrur (H8564) — a pillar, a heap set up; rendered high heaps.
Hebrew mesillah (H4546) — a raised road, a highway; the way to be kept in mind.
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, to return; turn again, twice.
Hebrew nethibah (H5410) — a path; the old paths of Jeremiah 6:16.
usage: “set thee up waymarks” — mark the road on the way out.
“set thine heart toward the highway” — the direction kept in mind.
“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” — the counsel to the wandering.

pos: n. pl. (guardians having charge of a minor heir)
etymology: Greek epitropos, a steward or guardian — one entrusted with the care of a person or estate. Latin tutor, a protector or guardian, from tueri, to watch over. The legal sense is primary: not a teacher, but the custodian of a child heir.
biblical_def: But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. Paul is making a legal argument and the vocabulary is technical. Under Roman practice an heir who was still a minor was placed under guardians and stewards; he owned the whole estate in principle and controlled none of it in practice, and the arrangement ended on a date the father had fixed. Paul says so in the preceding verse: the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all. That is his picture of the covenant people under the law — genuine heirs, under genuine tutelage, waiting on a date they did not set. The application follows: even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world. And then the hinge of the whole passage turns on that appointed date, which arrived exactly when the Father had determined, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. Two things follow for the reading of the Old Testament. The law was not a mistake or a rival system; a guardian is appointed by the father and acts with his authority, which is why Paul calls the law holy, and just, and good. And the guardianship was always temporary by design, terminating not at the heir's initiative but at the father's appointed time.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a guardian; one who has the charge of a child or pupil and his estate; one who instructs.
webster_full: TUTOR, n. A guardian; one who has the charge of a child or pupil and his estate.
TUTOR, n. An instructor; one who has the care of instructing another in various branches of learning.
GOVERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority; a tutor; one who has the care of a young man.
GUARDIAN, n. One who has the care of an orphan or minor, and of his estate, by legal appointment.
HEIR, n. The man who succeeds or is to succeed another in the possession of property.
scriptures: Galatians 4:2
But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father.
Galatians 4:1
Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all;
Galatians 4:3
Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:
Galatians 4:5
To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
corruption_summary: The law is treated either as a discarded system belonging to a superseded people or as still binding in its ceremonial administration; Paul makes it a guardianship appointed by the Father and ended at his appointed time.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomian readings take Galatians 4 as proof that the law has simply been abolished, and with it any continuing rule for the Christian life. The image will not carry it. A tutor appointed by the father is not an enemy, and the ending of a guardianship does not mean the guardian was wrong. Paul says elsewhere that the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good, and that faith does not make it void but establishes it. What ended was the covenant administration under which the heir was kept as a servant; what remains is the moral law, written now in the heart under the new covenant.

The opposite error keeps the guardianship running past its term. Wherever Christians are placed under ceremonial requirements — dietary law, festival calendars, circumcision, or their functional equivalents in later church tradition — the minor is being returned to the nursery after the father has declared him of age. That was precisely the Galatian error, and Paul's response to it is the sharpest language in his letters. The doctrine at stake is adoption: the point of the passage is that the appointed time came, the Son was sent, and the heirs received the standing of sons. To go back under tutors is to deny that the date arrived.
roots_summary: Greek epitropos (G2012), a guardian or steward; oikonomos (G3623), a house-manager; prothesmia (G4287), an appointed time; huiothesia (G5206), adoption of sons.
roots_lines: Greek epitropos (G2012) — a guardian entrusted with a minor; rendered tutors.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward of an estate; rendered governors.
Greek prothesmia (G4287) — a time appointed beforehand; its only occurrence, and the hinge of the argument.
Greek huiothesia (G5206) — the placing as a son, adoption; what the appointed time brought.
Greek paidagogos (G3807) — a child-conductor; rendered schoolmaster in the parallel at Galatians 3:24.
usage: “under tutors and governors” — a legal guardianship, not schooling.
“until the time appointed of the father” — a date the heir did not set.
“that we might receive the adoption of sons” — what the date brought.

pos: adj. (able to be seen; perceptible to the eye)
etymology: Greek horatos, able to be seen, from horao, to see. Latin visibilis, from videre, to see. Paul pairs it with its negative, aoratos, invisible, to make a statement about the totality of creation.
biblical_def: For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him. The pairing visible and invisible is doing a specific job: it closes every gap. Paul is not listing two categories of thing but using a pair of opposites to mean everything, and he reinforces it three times in one sentence — all things, in heaven and in earth, by him and for him. The four terms that follow are names for angelic and spiritual ranks, and their inclusion is the point of the verse in its setting. The Colossian error involved the worship of angels and an interest in intermediary powers; Paul answers by putting every such power on the created side of the line, made by Christ and made for him. Nothing in the unseen realm is uncreated, and nothing is outside his ownership. The preceding verse has already established who is speaking of: who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature — and firstborn here is a title of rank and heirship, not of origin, since the one by whom all things were created cannot himself be among the things created. The verse following completes the claim: and he is before all things, and by him all things consist. John says the same at the beginning of his Gospel: all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): perceivable by the eye; that can be seen; apparent; open; conspicuous.
webster_full: VISIBLE, a. Perceivable by the eye; that can be seen; as, the sun and stars are visible.
VISIBLE, a. Apparent; open; conspicuous; as the visible church.
INVISIBLE, a. That cannot be seen; imperceptible by the sight.
CREATE, v.t. To produce; to bring into being from nothing; to cause to exist.
DOMINION, n. Sovereign or supreme authority; the power of governing and controlling; an order of angels.
scriptures: Colossians 1:16

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
Colossians 1:15
Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:
Colossians 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
John 1:3
All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
corruption_summary: The deity of Christ is denied by reading firstborn as first-created, and the unseen realm is either dismissed as mythology or treated as a field for speculation; Paul places all of it on the created side and under Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Arianism in its ancient and modern forms rests on the firstborn of every creature, read as though Christ were the first item in the list of created things. Verse 16 refutes it in the next breath: by him were ALL things created, and a creator of all things is not one of them. Prototokos in Scripture denotes rank and inheritance rather than sequence — David is called God's firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth, and he was the youngest of eight sons. Nicaea confessed what this passage teaches: begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father. The dictionary holds the eternal generation of the Son and the full deity of Christ without reservation.

On the unseen realm there are two failures and the text answers both. The materialist reading treats thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers as first-century mythology, which requires deleting a great deal of the New Testament. The opposite failure is the fascination Colossae itself displayed — an appetite for angelic hierarchies, intermediaries, and the mapping of spiritual ranks, which recurs in every generation that finds ordinary doctrine dull. Paul's handling is the model: he affirms that the powers are real, names them, and then makes the only point that matters about them. They were made by Christ and for Christ, and the believer who is in him has nothing to negotiate with them.
roots_summary: Greek horatos (G3707), visible; aoratos (G517), invisible; prototokos (G4416), firstborn; sunistemi (G4921), to hold together or consist.
roots_lines: Greek horatos (G3707) — able to be seen; rendered visible, its only occurrence.
Greek aoratos (G517) — unseen, invisible; used of God himself in the previous verse.
Greek prototokos (G4416) — firstborn; a title of rank and heirship, not of origin.
Greek ktizo (G2936) — to create; the verb whose subject is Christ and whose object is all things.
Greek sunistemi (G4921) — to hold together; by him all things consist.
usage: “visible and invisible” — a pair of opposites meaning everything.
“thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers” — the unseen ranks, created.
“all things were created by him, and for him” — the claim stated twice.
